Madam Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honor to present our annual report and two thematic studies in my capacity as the chair of the Expert Mechanism on the Right to Development. Since our last report to this Council, the Expert Mechanism has held two sessions, actively involving Member States, civil society, experts, and practitioners. We have also engaged with international negotiations to promote full consideration of the right to development and continued to closely coordinate with the chair of the Intergovernmental Working Group on the Right to Development and the Special Rapporteur, among others. During our tenth session in Geneva last year, the expert mechanism undertook meaningful exchanges about ways in which the right to development could be featured in ongoing international discussions, agreements, and instruments. We discussed two draft studies and held six interactive thematic dialogues aimed at drawing upon experiences, good practices, and strategies to address pressing global challenges. At our 11th session in New York earlier this year, We explored how member states and other stakeholders could face the new global context at multilateral and national levels, looking ahead to the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development. We discussed two draft studies and held three in-focus discussion. As a result, we issued a package of recommendations for mainstreaming the right to development in the outcome document of the Financing for Development Fourth Conference. These documents are available on our website. Madam Chair, I'm pleased to further present today two thematic studies, Operationalizing the Right to Development in International Development Cooperation, led by my fellow expert, Meha Kanade, and climate justice, sustainability, and the right to development, which I led myself. They're contained in documents A.HRC.60/94 and A.HRC.60/95, respectively. The first study explores the cross-cutting normative principles of the right to development that can be mainstreamed across cooperation practices. It focuses on bilateral and triangular cooperation, providing lessons that can apply to other practices, including development banks, financial institutions, and trade organizations. The study underscores the importance of international cooperation in realizing human rights and sustainable development against the contexts where the 2030 agenda is derailed, Progress on poverty and hunger has stalled or even reversed, and many developing countries face a monumental financing gap, being either in or at risk of debt distress. Global partnership and enhanced cooperation are critical, especially for least developed countries and other low-income countries. But when cooperation is ineffective, it can be harmful to the right to development of individuals and peoples. In most cases, conditionalities undermine the recipient's development priorities and goals, as well as its welfare policies, and certain trade and investment agreements can limit the governance and policy space of states. The study analyzes the principles of effective, North-South, South-South, and triangular cooperation, identifying good practices in each context. It further shows that operationalizing the right to development at all stages of development cooperation can help to ensure effectiveness, making it possible to make a conscious effort to humanize cooperation. Some of the normative principles of the right to development that the study elaborates are Development is an inalienable right of all individuals and people, not a privilege. The right holders should be able to self-determine their priorities. The process by which outcomes are achieved as important as the outcomes. Receiving states have a duty to respect, protect, and fulfill the right to development. States must not obstruct others' right to development, including uncooperative practices and unilateral coercive measures. States able to assist should do so in line with their extraterritorial obligations to realize the right to development. Cooperation is a duty, not charity. Impact assessments are essential. Mutual accountability is crucial, including transparency, public availability of information, and remedies. The second study titled Climate Justice, Sustainability and the Right to Development examines how the right to development can be effectively incorporated into established and emerging climate practices and policies. It reconciles environmental sustainability and development aspirations. Climate justice is presented not only as a guiding framework but as a central objective for meaningful and effective climate action. The study sets out how each core principle of the right to development, such as equality, meaningful participation, self-determination, and international cooperation, can be applied in a context of climate action to enable more equitable outcomes, strengthen legitimacy, and address accountability gaps. The study offers a normative framework and a set of practical strategies to advance climate justice, highlighting promising practices. It offers concrete recommendations to address critical gaps in climate governance and finance, including the establishment of climate finance hubs to enhance coordination and provide technical assistance. the creation of a dedicated climate justice fund, and the appointment of climate justice ombudspersons at both national and international levels. A reform of global intellectual property rights regimes, which currently restrict equitable and timely access to vital technologies for climate mitigation and adaptation. And finally, broader structural reforms of the global financial system international trade policies, and transfer of technology. Climate action must respond to lived realities, priorities, and aspirations of those most affected by the climate crisis. The expert mechanism calls for aligning climate strategies with right to development principles to enhance legitimacy, bridge accountability gaps, and deliver more equitable and impactful solutions. We trust that the two studies will serve as valuable contributions to the deliberations of the Human Rights Council and offer practical guidance in advancing the right to development. Recently, important progress has been achieved through the appointment of the Federal Anti-Slavery Commissioner, provision of responses to the review of the Modern Slavery Act, and numerous promising projects, including the Support for Trafficked People program, the workplace justice visa and the strengthening reporting protections pilot scheme. I also warmly welcome Australia's regional and global leadership through initiatives such as the Bali Process and ASEAN Act. Nevertheless, challenges remain which must be fully addressed. These include high risks of exploitation faced by migrant workers, including those under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility Scheme, as well as asylum seekers. Further challenges lie in ensuring adequate labour inspections, stronger regulation over labour hire and recruitment agents, as well as in guaranteeing equal access to basic protection and essential services such as healthcare. legal assistance and social support. Concerns also persist in relation to the segregated employment and sub-minimum wages for persons with disabilities, the enduring impact of colonial legacies on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, ongoing discrimination experienced by sex workers and inconsistencies in legislative and protection frameworks across states and territories. In addition, while the Modern Slavery Act has improved awareness among businesses, its limited enforcement powers and the absence of mandatory human rights due diligence provision continue to restrict its practical impact. Nevertheless, in light of Australia's significant achievements to date and its continued constructive engagement with civil society, workers' organizations, and businesses, I believe that these challenges can be overcome through concerted action. With regard to other country visits, I just returned from Brazil, and my full report will be presented next year. I also welcome invitations extended by Serbia and Guatemala. Madam Vice-President, I now would like to provide a summary of my new thematic report on the worst forms of child labour. As you know, under SDG target 8.7, states and the international community pledged themselves to end child labor in all its forms by the end of this year. However, estimated 138 million children remain subjected to labor worldwide, with 54 million in hazardous forms. In my report, I documented widespread and diverse forms of hazardous work, particularly in sectors such as agriculture, livestock, fishery, construction, mining, and domestic work, most of which are informal in nature. Sexual exploitation, which has dramatically increased in a digital environment. Recruitment in armed conflicts and exploitation in criminal activities such as drug production and trafficking. The persistence of worst forms of child labour stems from structural, legal, economic and social barriers, and I will name just a few examples in this regard. Many national laws fail to address new challenges such as digital exploitation, and the informal economy is poorly regulated, which facilitates exploitation and abuse. Furthermore, lack of reliable data on child labour hampers victim identification and accountability, and child protection systems, particularly trauma-informed services, are fragmented and underfunded. Also, children forced into crime or prostitution are often punished rather than protected, undermining the principle of non-punishment. In addition, many businesses fail to identify child labour risks in their value chains. And finally, poverty, armed conflict, displacement, gender inequality, a lack of access to education and social protection, and the demand for cheap labour all perpetuate child labour in all regions of the world. I wish to acknowledge, however, that several promising initiatives have been implemented by States in order to address these ongoing challenges to eliminate child labour in all its forms. For example, many States have amended their legal frameworks in line with the international standards, including the creation of a list of hazardous work and the prohibition of online and offline sexual and criminal exploitation of children. Others have also strengthened human rights due diligence and other measures to compel businesses to identify and mitigate the risks of child labour. In addition, a number of States have enhanced institutional frameworks by establishing inter-ministerial or agency bodies dedicated to identifying the worst forms of child labour and protecting victims, including securing their access to justice and remedies. Finally, I wish to acknowledge the crucial role played by civil society and workers' organizations, as they are at the forefront of addressing child labor in all its forms, despite the fact that many are suffering from shrinking funding and civic space. Excellencies and distinguished delegates, despite these positive developments, the 2025 target is unattainable under the current trajectories. To move forward, states must prioritize prevention of child labor through education, social protection, and labor rights, strengthen enforcement and accountability, expand international cooperation, and adopt a smart mix of measures to strengthen human rights due diligence obligations for businesses. It is of critical importance that children themselves especially survivors of labour, sexual and criminal exploitation are meaningfully included in policy design and development. Madam Vice-President, next year marks the centenary of the Slavery Convention adopted here in Geneva in 1926. I urge the Council to seize this opportunity to renew the collective commitment and action for the elimination of contemporary forms of slavery in all countries. I also call on you to provide much-needed funding support for the UN Voluntary Trust Fund for Contemporary Forms of Slavery. It issues grants to civil society organizations which provide life-saving support to victims and survivors, but this year it has so far only received one single small contribution, and I count on your support in this regard. Finally, this is my last interactive dialogue as a Special Rapporteur. I would like to thank the Council, Member States, as well as non-governmental stakeholders for their engagement and support during my tenure. There is still so much more to be done to eliminate contemporary forms of slavery, but I am confident that the next appointee will take the mandate even further, and I would like to wish him or her every success. In the meantime, I look forward to fulfilling my duties for the remainder of my term. Thank you very much for your attention.
